question: One member of the Swiss Federal Council serves as President of the Swiss Confederation for one year at a time. That President chairs the meetings of the Federal Council and represents the federal government externally. How does the presidency affect that member's decision-making power?

options.A: The President carries considerably more decision-making power, because the President chairs the meetings and can act for the Council alone.
options.B: The President gains extra decision-making power in foreign affairs only, as the Confederation's external representative.
options.C: The President has hardly any more decision-making power than the other members of the Federal Council.
options.D: The President gains a casting vote, which breaks any deadlock in the Council in the President's favour.

source_quote: In contrast to other countries, the President of the Confederation in Switzerland has hardly any more decision-making power than the other members of the Federal Council.
notes: Swiss-specific: the rotating presidency is a chairmanship, not a head-of-state office. Traps the German Bundeskanzler and US presidential models.

question: The Federal Chancellor is sometimes referred to in Swiss media as the 'eighth Federal Councillor'. What is the Federal Chancellor's actual role?

options.A: A supporting and advisory role for the Federal Council, rather than a seat in it.
options.B: A voting member of the Federal Council, counted among the seven when decisions are taken.
options.C: The head of state, who represents Switzerland towards foreign governments.
options.D: The head of the Federal Administration, supervising its seven departments.

source_quote: There is often talk of an 'eighth Federal Councillor', the Federal Chancellor, who has a supporting and advisory role for the Federal Council.
notes: The Chancellor is neither head of state (the rotating President) nor head of government (the Federal Council as a collegial body). Common model failure: importing the German Bundeskanzler.

question: When the seven members of the Swiss Federal Council deal with an item of business at their meeting, how do they proceed to a decision?

options.A: The President tables a proposal and the other six members confirm it unless three of them object.
options.B: The members vote first on the available options, and the majority position becomes the Federal Council's decision.
options.C: The item is first referred to the cantons for a consultative vote, and the Federal Council then implements the result.
options.D: The members first seek a common solution, and only vote if they fail to reach one.

source_quote: They discuss the items on the agenda at the Federal Council meeting and seek a common solution. Only if it does not reach a solution, does the Federal Council vote.
notes: Consensus-before-vote is the defining feature of the Swiss collegial executive; no majority-vote casting exists in the normal case.

question: The National Council and the Council of States of the Swiss Parliament take most of their decisions separately. When is a decision of the Federal Assembly final?

options.A: As soon as the National Council has approved it, because it is the larger of the two chambers.
options.B: Only when both chambers reach the same conclusion; otherwise the 'resolution of differences procedure' follows.
options.C: When a simple majority of the members of both chambers added together votes for it.
options.D: When the Federal Council endorses it, since the Federal Council sits between the two chambers.

source_quote: Parliament's decisions are only final if the National Council and the Council of States reach the same conclusion. Otherwise, the two chambers must follow the 'resolution of differences procedure' in an attempt to reach an agreement.
notes: Neither chamber is dominant — a bicameral equal-footing design with no overrider, unlike most second chambers.

question: How many seats does the Council of States, the upper chamber of the Swiss Parliament, have?

options.A: 46 seats
options.B: 52 seats
options.C: 26 seats
options.D: 40 seats

source_quote: The Swiss Parliament has 200 seats in the National Council and 46 seats in the Council of States.
notes: 46 = 20 cantons x 2 seats + 6 former half-cantons x 1 seat. 52 is the intuitive-but-wrong 26 x 2. Sourced from S003 (S026 holds the same content).

question: Which cantons are entitled to only one seat in the Council of States?

options.A: Ticino, Jura and Geneva
options.B: Glarus, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Obwalden
options.C: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft
options.D: Valais, Uri and Zug

source_quote: The former half-cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft are only entitled to one.
notes: The six are all former half-cantons; the historical reason is a leftover of the old Confederation's status. Source spells the Basel cantons without hyphens.

question: To force an optional referendum against a law passed by the Swiss Parliament, how many valid signatures must be collected, and within what deadline?

options.A: 100,000 signatures within 100 days
options.B: 50,000 signatures within 18 months
options.C: 100,000 signatures within 18 months
options.D: 50,000 signatures within 100 days

source_quote: collect 50,000 valid signatures within 100 days of the publication of the new legislation
notes: Pair with K011: the optional referendum is 50,000 signatures / 100 days; the federal popular initiative is 100,000 / 18 months.

question: A campaign team is gathering signatures for an optional referendum against a federal law. Which restriction applies to the individual signature lists?

options.A: Each list must carry at least 500 signatures from one and the same canton.
options.B: A single list may only contain signatures from people of the same commune, because the communes are the first to check the signatures.
options.C: A voter may sign only one list per canton, and any duplicate signature invalidates the whole list.
options.D: Each list must be countersigned by the mayor of the commune before it can be submitted.

source_quote: A further requirement is that any given signature list may contain only the signatures of persons from the same commune – because the communes are the first to check the signatures.
notes: Counter-intuitive administrative detail: signature gathering is decentralised to the commune for verification. The same per-commune form rule applies to popular initiatives.

question: The voting age in Switzerland is 18 at federal level, and each canton is free to set its own age for cantonal and communal votes. Where may 16- and 17-year-olds vote?

options.A: In Glarus, at cantonal and communal level — they may vote but not stand for election.
options.B: Nowhere, because no canton may set the voting age below 18.
options.C: In Glarus, Bern and Basel-Stadt, but only in cantonal and not in communal votes.
options.D: In any canton that chooses to allow it, since cantons are entirely free to set the age.

source_quote: Currently Glarus is the only canton to allow 16- and 17-year-olds to vote at cantonal and communal level, but not to stand for election.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE and time-specific: Glarus is named as the sole canton on the page as accessed 2026-10-12. Canton is named explicitly in the stem.

question: In Switzerland the separation of powers applies at federal, cantonal and communal level. May one person hold office in more than one of the three branches of the Swiss state at the same time?

options.A: Yes, but only where the second office is at communal level and is unpaid.
options.B: Yes, provided the two offices are held in two different cantons.
options.C: Yes, because judges are treated as belonging to the executive rather than to the judiciary.
options.D: No — a person may belong to only one of the three branches of the state at any one time.

source_quote: A person may belong to only one of the three branches of the state (at federal, cantonal or communal level) at any one time.
notes: Branch incompatibility. It is why a Federal Councillor cannot sit in Parliament or on the Federal Supreme Court.

question: How many valid signatures must be collected for a federal popular initiative, and within what time limit?

options.A: 50,000 signatures within 100 days
options.B: 100,000 signatures within 18 months
options.C: 100,000 signatures within 100 days
options.D: 50,000 signatures within 18 months

source_quote: For an initiative to come to fruition, it must be signed by 100,000 voters within 18 months.
notes: Direct democracy threshold. Contrast with K007: referendum 50,000 / 100 days.

question: How many members must the committee of a federal popular initiative have, and what must each of them satisfy?

options.A: At least three members, all of whom must be Swiss citizens resident in Switzerland.
options.B: At least seven members, with no upper limit on the size of the committee.
options.C: At least seven and at most twenty-seven members, each of whom is eligible to vote in Switzerland.
options.D: Between seven and twenty-seven members, at least half of whom must come from different language regions.

source_quote: The initiative committee must have at least 7 and no more than 27 members, who each must be eligible to vote in Switzerland.
notes: There is both a floor (7) and a ceiling (27) — models frequently recall only the lower bound or invent a minimum of 3.

question: Across the Swiss cantons, who presides over the cantonal government, and what does that role carry with it?

options.A: The population of the canton elects a cantonal president directly for a four-year term, with decision-making powers equal to those of the other members.
options.B: The Federal Council appoints a cantonal president for a two-year term.
options.C: The presidency passes to the longest-serving member and carries substantial additional powers.
options.D: The presidency usually rotates from year to year and carries no privileges beyond chairing the cantonal government's meetings.

source_quote: Cantonal governments usually have a different president each year - the position rotating according to the length of time the government members have been in office. The president does not enjoy any special privileges or status, apart from chairing cantonal government meetings.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE: rotation follows length of service, so the source says 'usually'. Phrased as the general cantonal pattern, never as a universal seven-member rule.

question: How does the size of a cantonal parliament vary in Switzerland? Give the two figures cited on the federal ch.ch portal.

options.A: Appenzell Innerrhoden has 50 members and Zurich has 180.
options.B: Appenzell Innerrhoden has 28 members and Zurich has 180.
options.C: Appenzell Innerrhoden has 50 members and Zurich has 200.
options.D: Every canton has 100 members, with seats assigned in proportion to population.

source_quote: The number of members of parliament varies from canton to canton. It is usually proportional to the population of the canton. The parliament of Appenzell Innerrhoden currently has 50 members while the Zurich parliament has 180 members.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE and time-specific ('currently' as of the 2026-10-12 page). Both cantons are named explicitly, per the cantonal-variation rule.

question: In Swiss popular votes, which proposals require a so-called 'double majority' rather than a simple majority of the voters?

options.A: Federal laws and most international treaties.
options.B: Amendments to the Constitution and decisions to join a supranational community.
options.C: Amendments to the Constitution only — joining a supranational community requires a popular majority alone.
options.D: Any proposal on which more than one canton votes.

source_quote: But the decision to amend the constitution or join a supranational community requires a so-called double majority. Such a proposal is accepted only if both the majority of voters (popular majority) as well as the majority of cantons say yes.
notes: The supranational-community limb is the non-obvious half — it is what would apply to any EU accession question, which Switzerland is not part of.

question: When the cantonal majority is counted for a constitutional amendment or a vote on joining a supranational community, what weight does each of the former half-cantons carry?

options.A: A full vote, the same as any other canton.
options.B: No vote at all, since they are no longer separate cantons.
options.C: Half a vote each.
options.D: Two votes each, reflecting their combined historic weight.

source_quote: The votes of the former half-cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each count as half a vote.
notes: The six former half-cantons weigh 0.5 each, so the cantonal majority is effectively a weighted 23-canton vote. Note this is a separate mechanism from the single Council of States seat they hold.

question: Switzerland is running e-voting trials. What numerical limits apply to how many voters may use them?

options.A: Up to 30% of eligible voters in any one canton, with a national cap of 10%.
options.B: Up to 10% of eligible voters in any one canton, with a national cap of 30%.
options.C: Up to 30% of eligible voters nationwide, with no separate cantonal cap.
options.D: No numerical cap at all — each canton decides freely how many of its voters may vote online.

source_quote: The scope of the trials is limited: a maximum of 30% of eligible voters are permitted to use e-voting in any particular canton, with the national cap set at 10%.
notes: The per-canton 30% / national 10% split is inverted from the intuitive reading. As accessed 2026-10-12; actual participation falls well below these quotas.

question: Apart from the Federal Supreme Court, how many further courts exercise judicial functions at the federal level in Switzerland, and which are they?

options.A: One — the Federal Constitutional Court.
options.B: Three — the Federal Criminal Court, the Federal Administrative Court and the Federal Patent Court.
options.C: Three — the Federal Criminal Court, the Federal Constitutional Court and the Federal Supreme Administrative Court.
options.D: Two — the Federal Criminal Court and the Federal Administrative Court.

source_quote: The Federal Criminal Court, the Federal Administrative Court and the Federal Patent Court are the three other courts at federal level.
notes: There is no separate Federal Constitutional Court — a common import from Germany (Bundesverfassungsgericht) or Austria. The Federal Patent Court is the genuinely non-obvious fourth federal court.

question: About how many items of business does the Swiss Federal Council deal with in a year?

options.A: around 250
options.B: around 25,000
options.C: around 2,500
options.D: around 250,000

source_quote: Each year the Federal Council deals with around 2,500 items of business.
notes: Replaces an earlier K019 (duration of the weekly meeting), which was rejected at manual review: three of its four options were implausible. This item tests the small size of the Swiss consensus executive - seven councillors handling ~2,500 items, against the tens of thousands a large national cabinet would process. Distractors span three orders of magnitude so each is a real candidate.

question: The Federal Chancellery supports the Federal Council but is neither the head of state nor the head of government. Which of the following is one of its actual duties in Switzerland?

options.A: Chairing the Federal Council meetings and representing it abroad.
options.B: Supervising the seven federal departments and their heads.
options.C: Adjudicating appeals against decisions of the federal authorities.
options.D: Organising federal elections and referendums, as guardian of the people's rights.

source_quote: As guardian of the people's rights, the Federal Chancellery organises federal elections and referendums.
notes: Precise delimitation: the Chancellery is the Federal Council's staff office, not a head of state/government. Referendum and initiative committees submit their signatures to it.

question: Which languages does the Federal Chancellery ensure are used correctly and understandably in laws and official texts?

options.A: German, French, Italian, and sometimes Romansh or English
options.B: German and French only
options.C: German, French, Italian, Romansh and English in every case
options.D: The two or three languages most widely used in the canton concerned

source_quote: German, French, Italian, and sometimes Romansh or English: the Federal Chancellery ensures that laws and official texts are understandable and correct.
notes: Traps the assumption that a language-monitoring office would either cover only the two federal court languages or all five national languages on a mandatory basis.

question: Alongside organising federal elections and popular votes, which parties submit the signatures they have collected to the Federal Chancellery?

options.A: The Federal Supreme Court
options.B: Members of the Federal Assembly acting in united chambers
options.C: Referendum and initiative committees
options.D: The cantonal governments

source_quote: Along with the cantons, the Federal Chancellery organises federal elections and popular votes. Referendum and initiative committees submit the signatures they collect to the Federal Chancellery.
notes: Separates the Chancellery's organising role from its intake role, and separates both from the cantons' own task of organising the vote.

question: In addition to coordinating the digital transformation of the federal administration, what does the Federal Chancellery do to support Federal Council policy decisions?

options.A: It audits the federal administration on behalf of the Federal Assembly
options.B: It keeps abreast of international trends and develops scenarios for the future
options.C: It negotiates Switzerland's international treaties on behalf of the Federal Council
options.D: It verifies the constitutional compatibility of acts adopted by the Federal Assembly

source_quote: The Federal Chancellery keeps abreast of international trends and develops scenarios for the future. This helps the Federal Council make policy decisions.
notes: The Chancellery is a staff office, not a political negotiator, a constitutional reviewer or an audit body; each distractor assigns it a function belonging to another federal body.

question: As Switzerland's highest court, the Federal Supreme Court acts as the final instance on appeals against which decisions?

options.A: Decisions of any cantonal court, at first and second instance
options.B: Decisions of the cantonal governments and of cantonal administrative authorities
options.C: Only decisions of the Federal Criminal Court and the Federal Administrative Court
options.D: Decisions of the highest cantonal courts and of the three other federal courts

source_quote: It rules as the final instance on all appeals against decisions of the highest cantonal courts, the Federal Criminal Court, the Federal Administrative Court and the Federal Patent Court.
notes: Tests the appellate ceiling: not every cantonal decision, only the top cantonal tier, and not only the federal criminal and administrative courts. D is a near-miss subset.

question: Where are most criminal cases in Switzerland decided in the first instance?

options.A: By cantonal courts
options.B: By the Federal Criminal Court
options.C: By the Federal Supreme Court
options.D: By the Federal Administrative Court

source_quote: Most criminal cases are decided in the first instance by cantonal courts.
notes: Counterintuitive for anyone importing a model where a national criminal court is the ordinary first-instance criminal body; the Federal Criminal Court is a specialist exception.

question: A case concerns money laundering and organised crime with an international dimension. Which federal body hears such cases?

options.A: The Federal Supreme Court sitting as a criminal first-instance court
options.B: The Federal Criminal Court
options.C: The Federal Administrative Court
options.D: The Federal Patent Court

source_quote: The Federal Criminal Court hears criminal cases involving offences against federal interests, explosives offences, international cases of white-collar crime, cases relating to organised crime, corruption and money laundering, and offences related to civil aviation or war material.
notes: Distinguishes the four federal courts by subject matter. D invents a criminal first-instance division of the Supreme Court, a structure familiar from other countries.

question: Which of the following kinds of case falls within the jurisdiction of the Federal Administrative Court?

options.A: A challenge to the legal validity of a patent for a technical innovation
options.B: A criminal case involving offences against federal interests
options.C: An appeal against a federal decision of principle in an asylum case
options.D: An appeal against a cantonal court's ruling in a civil dispute

source_quote: The Federal Administrative Court rules on appeals against decisions made by authorities of the Federal Administration. Some of the issues may be controversial from both a social and political standpoint. Examples include decisions of principle in asylum-related cases or on major transport and infrastructure projects.
notes: Each distractor is a real Swiss jurisdiction routed to the wrong court: civil appeals to the Supreme Court, patents to the Patent Court, federal criminal offences to the Federal Criminal Court.

question: Which body decides whether e-voting trials take place in a canton and which voters are eligible to take part in them?

options.A: The Federal Chancellery
options.B: The Federal Assembly
options.C: The Federal Supreme Court
options.D: Each canton, on its own

source_quote: Every canton decides for itself whether to conduct e-voting trials. The cantons also decide which voters would be eligible to participate in the trials.
notes: Proves cantonal autonomy inside a federally regulated area. B and D exploit the Chancellery's role in organising votes and the Supreme Court's constitutional role.

question: A voter casts a ballot electronically in an e-voting trial and afterwards sends a postal ballot using the same voter identification card. What is the result?

options.A: The postal ballot replaces the electronic vote
options.B: The postal ballot is not counted
options.C: Both the electronic vote and the postal ballot are counted
options.D: Both the electronic vote and the postal ballot are cancelled

source_quote: Once you have cast your vote electronically, your voter identification card will be recorded and blocked for other forms of voting (by post or at a polling station). You cannot vote again at a polling station using a voter identification card that has already been used for e-voting. Votes sent by post with a voter identification card that has already been used will not be counted.
notes: The card-blocking mechanism is the anti-double-vote control; B and C are the natural guesses from models trained on jurisdictions that reconcile rather than discard.

question: Which of the following is a task of a cantonal parliament in Switzerland?

options.A: Appointing the members of the cantonal government each year
options.B: Ruling on appeals against decisions of cantonal administrative authorities
options.C: Supervising the activity of the cantonal government
options.D: Managing cantonal affairs and planning cantonal projects

source_quote: Last but not least, the cantonal parliament supervises the activity of the cantonal government.
notes: B is the cantonal government's own core task and C is a plausible overreach; D confuses parliamentary oversight with judicial review.

question: Who chairs the meetings of a cantonal parliament?

options.A: A member of that parliament, elected to the presidency each year
options.B: The president of the cantonal government for that year
options.C: The president of the Confederation
options.D: The longest-serving member of the cantonal parliament

source_quote: Parliament annually elects one of its members to be president. The president's duties include chairing the meetings of parliament.
notes: Traps the assumption that the executive heads the legislature too, or that the federal president presides over cantonal business. Rotating annual presidency parallels the federal arrangement.

question: Which statement correctly describes how a cantonal parliament meets?

options.A: It meets roughly once a month, behind closed doors
options.B: It meets weekly, in public, as the Federal Assembly does
options.C: It meets behind closed doors, and its minutes are not public
options.D: It meets roughly once a month, in public

source_quote: Council members holds regular, scheduled meetings, usually once a month. These meetings and their minutes are generally public.
notes: Contrasts the legislature's public monthly rhythm with the cantonal government's behind-closed-doors meetings; C borrows the federal weekly cadence.

question: How many members does a cantonal government in Switzerland have?

options.A: Between nine and twelve
options.B: Between five and seven
options.C: Between three and five
options.D: Between seven and nine

source_quote: There are between five and seven members in each cantonal government.
notes: Establishes the cantonal counterpart to the seven-member Federal Council, which a model tends to over-generalise to cantonal level.

question: A member of a cantonal government privately disagrees with a decision the government has taken. What is that member required to do?

options.A: Ask the cantonal parliament to reverse the decision
options.B: Abstain in public and distance themselves from the decision
options.C: Defend the government's position publicly, whatever their own opinion
options.D: Resign from the cantonal government immediately

source_quote: All members of the cantonal government must defend the position of the collegial body, regardless of their personal opinion.
notes: Collegiality binds the cantonal government exactly as it binds the Federal Council; B, C and D are all plausible reactions from a cabinet-style mental model.

question: How do the meetings of a cantonal government usually take place?

options.A: Behind closed doors
options.B: In public, with the minutes published
options.C: Behind closed doors, but minuted and published
options.D: In public, but only after the agenda has been published

source_quote: The members of the cantonal government hold regular scheduled meetings, usually behind closed doors.
notes: Pairs with K162: the same canton legislates in public but executes behind closed doors. C is the tempting half-right compromise.

question: What does the Federal Administration consist of?

options.A: The seven federal departments, the Federal Chancellery and the Federal Supreme Court
options.B: The seven federal departments alone
options.C: The Federal Chancellery and the seven Federal Council members
options.D: The seven federal departments together with the Federal Chancellery

source_quote: Each of the seven members of the Federal Council is head of one of the seven federal departments, which together with the Federal Chancellery make up the Federal Administration.
notes: B wrongly folds a court into the executive, C drops the Chancellery, D confuses the people who lead the administration with the administration's parts.

question: What is the task of the Federal Supreme Court as Switzerland's highest court?

options.A: Binding courts in other states on the interpretation of treaties
options.B: Ensuring the uniform application of the law
options.C: Supervising the cantonal courts for the Federal Assembly
options.D: Approving federal legislation before it enters into force

source_quote: The Federal supreme Court is Switzerland's highest court. Its task is to ensure the uniform application of the law and to uphold the rights of ordinary people.
notes: D is the key trap: uniform application is an internal Swiss function, not a supranational preliminary-reference power as in the EU.

question: As highest court of appeal, the Federal Supreme Court also rules on which further kinds of dispute?

options.A: Preliminary references from cantonal courts on the interpretation of federal law, as in the European Union
options.B: Complaints by foreign states against federal measures taken in Switzerland
options.C: Disputes between individuals and the state, and between the Confederation and the cantons
options.D: References from cantonal courts on the interpretation of federal law

source_quote: As the highest court of appeal, it also rules on disputes between individuals and the state or between the Confederation and the cantons.
notes: Switzerland resolves federal-cantonal and state-citizen disputes domestically in its own apex court. C is the strongest distractor because it imports the CJEU's preliminary-reference role.

question: When was the separation of powers introduced in Switzerland?

options.A: In 1848, on the founding of the federal state
options.B: In 1874, when the optional referendum was introduced
options.C: In 1891, when the federal popular initiative was introduced
options.D: In 1948, after a total revision of the federal Constitution

source_quote: In Switzerland, the powers of the state are divided among the three branches of the state: the legislature, the executive and the judiciary. This separation was introduced in 1848 on the founding of the federal state, with the aim of preventing a concentration of power in individual persons or institutions.
notes: Dates the principle to the founding of the federal state, not to 1874 or 1891 (the direct-democracy instruments) or to a post-war revision.

question: In which cantons do foreign nationals have the right to vote at cantonal level, though not to stand for election?

options.A: Jura and Geneva
options.B: Neuchâtel and Basel-Stadt
options.C: Geneva and Vaud
options.D: Jura and Neuchâtel

source_quote: At the cantonal level, Jura and Neuchâtel grant the right to vote (but not to stand for election) to foreign nationals.
notes: High search cost and tests real cantonal variation; Geneva and Vaud are the intuitive French-speaking guesses and are not the cited pair.

question: Does a Swiss citizen living in Switzerland have to register in order to be entered on the electoral roll of their commune?

options.A: Yes, but only people holding a single nationality
options.B: No, the commune adds them automatically
options.C: Yes, at the commune's population office each year
options.D: Yes, with the cantonal government before the vote

source_quote: If you live in Switzerland, you do not need to register to vote: you will be added to the electoral register of your commune of residence as a matter of course as soon as you fulfil the conditions for being eligible to vote.
notes: Contrast with the explicit registration required of Swiss citizens abroad; an automatic-register premise is unusual compared with most EU systems.

question: A Swiss citizen living abroad can vote at federal level. How many cantons also extend cantonal voting rights to Swiss citizens abroad?

options.A: None of them
options.B: Only the French-speaking cantons
options.C: Half of them
options.D: All of them

source_quote: Half of the cantons grant the right to vote at cantonal level to Swiss citizens abroad.
notes: Federal voting rights abroad are universal, but the cantonal layer is split roughly down the middle; the page frames the result as a fraction, not a list.

question: Who elects the judges of the Federal Supreme Court in Switzerland?

options.A: The Federal Council
options.B: The cantonal governments
options.C: The Federal Chancellery
options.D: The Federal Assembly

source_quote: elect federal authorities, including the seven members of the Federal Council, the President of the Confederation, the Federal Chancellor and the judges of the Federal Supreme Court
notes: Parliament elects the government, the Chancellor AND the apex judges, so judicial appointments are a legislative act. B and D wrongly put appointments with the executive's staff office.

question: How many regular sessions does the Federal Assembly hold each year, and how long does each session last?

options.A: Four sessions of three weeks
options.B: Four sessions of two months
options.C: Two sessions of three weeks
options.D: Six sessions of one week

source_quote: The members of the two chambers meet during parliamentary sessions, which take place four times a year. Each session lasts three weeks.
notes: A calendar fact a model rarely has; distractors vary each component independently so a half-remembered figure is punished.

question: Beyond the Federal Council, the Federal Administration and the Federal Supreme Court, which other bodies does the Federal Assembly monitor?

options.A: Foreign states in their dealings with the Confederation
options.B: Bodies that perform federal tasks, such as Swiss Post
options.C: Cantonal governments, cantonal courts and communes
options.D: The Federal Chancellery and the federal administrative offices

source_quote: monitor the activities of the Federal Council, the Federal Administration, the Federal Supreme Court and other bodies that perform federal tasks, e.g. the Swiss Post or the Swiss Federal Railways.
notes: Federal oversight reaches beyond the classic branches into autonomous bodies with federal tasks; B is the canton-level confusion the whole source set is trying to prevent.

question: Can a federal popular initiative be used at federal level to demand a change to an existing federal law rather than to the Constitution?

options.A: Yes, but only for laws adopted before the entry into force of the 1999 Constitution
options.B: Yes, provided the Federal Assembly agrees to treat the proposal as constitutional
options.C: No, a federal popular initiative can concern only the Constitution
options.D: Yes, if the initiative is supported by a majority of the cantons

source_quote: A federal popular initiative concerns only the Constitution. In contrast to the position in some cantons, there is no procedure at federal level for amending existing laws or introducing new laws through an initiative.
notes: The sharpest federalism point in the corpus: some cantons have legislative initiatives, federal level does not. C and D invent conditional routes.

question: How far in advance of the vote on a federal popular initiative must the date be announced, and by whom?

options.A: The cantonal governments must announce it at least one year ahead
options.B: The Federal Council must announce it at least four months ahead
options.C: The Federal Assembly must announce it at least six months ahead
options.D: The Federal Chancellery must announce it at least three months ahead

source_quote: The Federal Council must announce the date of the vote at least four months in advance.
notes: The executive, not the Chancellery or Parliament, fixes the ballot date; C is the natural confusion with the Chancellery's vote-organising role.

question: Since the federal popular initiative was introduced in 1891, roughly what share of the initiatives put to the vote has been adopted?

options.A: Around 25 per cent
options.B: Around 50 per cent
options.C: Around 90 per cent
options.D: Around 10 per cent

source_quote: More than 200 initiatives have been voted on since then, and around 10 per cent have been adopted.
notes: Corrects the intuition that a successful signature-gathering initiative is usually a successful outcome; the low adoption rate is the point.

question: Parliament decides not only on laws but also on enactments that are not laws, such as decisions on international treaties. Can an optional referendum be launched against such a decision?

options.A: Yes, an optional referendum is possible
options.B: No, only amendments to the Constitution are put to a vote
options.C: No, because treaties are approved by the Federal Council alone
options.D: Yes, but only after a majority of the cantons has approved the treaty

source_quote: Parliament also decides on enactments that are not laws, for example decisions on international treaties between Switzerland and other countries. It is also possible to launch an optional referendum against these.
notes: The referendum right reaches further than formally legislated acts; B and C are the usual assumptions about treaty approval in a parliamentary system.

question: Two groups from different political camps both want to challenge the same federal law. How is that handled?

options.A: Both may initiate a referendum, but their signatures are counted separately
options.B: Only one group may challenge the law if the camps disagree
options.C: Both may initiate a referendum, and their signatures are counted
options.D: Only the group that registered first may challenge the law

source_quote: What is more, several groups can initiate a referendum against the same new or amended law – even though they might be from different political camps. The signatures collected are counted.
notes: Competing committees do not exclude each other; C is a near-miss that would also work in practice but is not what the page states.
